A single major in a three-year general Bachelor of Arts program consists of 36 credits in a subject area, normally 6 credits at the introductory level and 30 upper year credits (maximum of 48 credits allowed in discipline specific courses for most programs except for Fine Arts, Music, Community Economics & Social Development, and Community Development). A minimum grade of 60 percent is required in the introductory discipline-specific courses to declare a major in the specific discipline.  
A single major in a four year and/or honours Bachelor of Arts program consists of a minimum of 54-60 credits in a single discipline, normally 6 credits at the introductory level and 48-54 upper year credits (maximum of 78 credits allowed in discipline specific courses). A minimum grade of 60 percent is required in the introductory discipline-specific courses to declare a major in the specific discipline.

metadata.Section header 2: Single Majors

text: Commonly referred to as a 'double major,' a combined major is a Bachelor of Arts program wherein the student completes 30 credits in each of two disciplines for 3-year programs and 42 credits in each of two disciplines for 4-year programs. A combined major is not a second degree (see policies section), and not all program combinations are possible. Specific credit requirements vary by program. Students interested in a combined major should read more in the program-specific sections and consult with an academic advisor and the registrar's office.

metadata.Section header 2: Combined Majors

text: A specialization is a defined set of courses which provides students with specific expertise, knowledge, and/or practice and so further distinguishes the program in a recognizable way. Unlike minors, specializations are pathways which are specific to the major of a degree program, and appear on the parchment awarded upon graduation. For instance, a student majoring in Computer Science may choose to complete the specialization in Computer Game Technology.

metadata.Section header 2: Specializations

text:
A minor is awarded when a student in a degree program centers 18- 24 of their elective credits around a particular field of study. Minors are available to all students who have declared a major in another discipline. In all cases, students will be expected to respect course prerequisite requirements. Minors are to be completed concurrently with the student's major. A minimum grade of 60 percent is required in the introductory discipline-specific courses to declare a minor in the specific discipline. For exceptions regarding the number of required credits to satisfy the requirements of a minor or for specific course requirements, please refer to the discipline-specific sections for more information.  
Students interested in completing minors are strongly encouraged to work with an Academic Advisor to ensure eligibility and completion in a timely manner. For specific academic regulations about minors please see the regulation and policies chapter (Chapter 2).

metadata.Section header 2: Minors

text: Accounting, Anishinaabemowin, Anishinaabe Studies, Biology, Business, Community Economic and Social Development, Computer Science, Economics, English, French, Geography, Geomatics, History, Human Development, Human Resources Management, International Relations, Law and Justice, Mathematics, Marketing, Music, Political Science, Psychology, Public Policy and Administration, Sociology, Visual Art. Generally 24 credits in a subject are required to earn a minor, though there are some exceptions.

metadata.Section header 2: 3.6.1.1 Bachelor of Business Administration (Honours) - Single Major [BBA]

text:
To graduate with a Bachelor of Business Administration degree, a student must:  
1. complete 120 credits (72 credits in Business/Economics; 48 elective credits)
2. complete all core courses (72 credits) with a minimum core-course average of 70% and with a minimum grade in each core course of 60%.
3. complete 120 credits in no more than 162 credit attempts with an overall minimum average of 60% in those courses
4. A student failing to attain this minimum grade in any of the core courses must repeat such courses as soon as possible. Failure to do so will result in suspension from the program. A student is permitted to repeat a core course only once, except with the special permission of the Senate Committee on Academic Regulations and Petitions.

text: The CESD program provides students with a critical and holistic (economic, social, environmental, political, and cultural) understanding of the global and local relations in which people organize to improve their communities. The program emphasizes skills to work for just, inclusive, and sustainable communities, with a special emphasis on smaller urban, rural, Northern, Anishinaabe/First Nation/Indigenous communities in Northern Ontario and elsewhere. CESD delivers programming for two-degree programs, Community Development (CDEV) and Community Economic and Social Development (CESD), as well as a minor in CESD and two certificates: CESD and First Nation Social Policy and Community Development (FNSPCD). CESD is accredited by the Council for the Advancement of Native Development Officers (CANDO) and can contribute to the Economic Developers Association of Canada (EDAC)'s Ec.D. designation and graduates of the CESD degree program are eligible to apply to these bodies for certification.

text: The Bachelor of Social Work (BSW) program prepares students for generalist social work practice with individuals, families, groups, organizations, communities, and societies. The program has a particular focus on social work in and with Northern, rural, remote, Indigenous, and Franco-Ontarian communities. Graduates of the program will be prepared to practice anti-oppressive social work at the entry level with diverse populations in a Canadian context.

metadata.Section header 2: 3.6.10.1 Overview

text:
The rich and innovative curriculum reflects a sound generalist program, while maintaining a focus on newer directions in social work. Students will use anti-colonial, structural, Indigenous, and feminist and anti-racism approaches to critically analyse the ways that social contexts shape personal and social problems. Graduates will have a deep awareness of how their personal experiences are embedded in social structures. The program includes a 700-hour field placement that will link social work concepts, values, and theory to practice.  
The Bachelor of Social Work program is accredited by the Canadian Association for Social Work Education (CASWE).
